web_evidence.note: A university-hosted literary thesis explicitly identifies third-person point of view and supports it with sustained opening narration about Jonathan as “he.”

web_evidence.title: Jonathan Livingston Seagull Study Guide
web_evidence.note: The guide lists the work’s point of view as third-person and distinguishes the original three-part edition from the later fourth-part edition.

web_evidence.title: Richard Bach Writing Styles in Jonathan Livingston Seagull
web_evidence.note: The point-of-view section describes a third-person past-tense narrator who follows Jonathan across the story’s Earth, exile, and heaven episodes.

web_evidence.title: Letters to the Editor: “Get Off My Bach!”
web_evidence.note: A contemporaneous discussion states that Jonathan is consistently referred to in the third person throughout the book, directly addressing whole-book narration.

search_log: Searched “Jonathan Livingston Seagull Richard Bach excerpt publisher PDF,” “first chapter excerpt,” “point of view,” “third person narrator,” and “scholarly analysis.”

Opened and assessed LitCharts, eNotes, BookRags, GradeSaver, a university-repository thesis, and a contemporaneous Dialogue journal letter; the usable sources consistently identified third-person narration.

Checked the official Simon & Schuster page and Google Books record/preview; they verified the title and 1970 edition but did not expose enough continuous prose or explicit POV analysis to use as person evidence.

Searched specifically for first-person, alternating narration, frame structure, Google Books, and Internet Archive evidence. Casual student slides and an interview transcript asserted first person without textual support and contradicted the opened text and stronger analyses, so they were treated as low-quality dead ends.
Found downloadable full-text copies on nonpublisher sites but did not rely on them as authorized Tier A evidence.
person_note: The controlling narrator is a nonparticipating third-person voice centered closely on Jonathan and able to report his thoughts and development. The diagnostic event passages and substantial dialogue framing agree with the scholarly analysis and several independent whole-book descriptions. First-, second-, and inclusive-person pronouns in the quotes are local character speech or thought, not autonomous narrative sections. No credible evidence of an alternating or participating narrator was found; the main limitation is the absence of an accessible authorized sustained excerpt, offset by the university analysis, repeated quote evidence, and multiple explicit whole-book sources.
